title.narrative: Collaboration for Harm Reduction and Alcohol Safety in the Environment in Southern Africa (CHASE-SA)
NIHR158821: Harmful alcohol use in Southern Africa: studying drivers of drinking for effective intervention

description.narrative:
Harmful alcohol use is substantial problem globally with negative impacts on health/wellbeing. The alcohol industry is a key driver of consumption/harms. It has responded to reduced consumption in many high-income countries (from increased regulation) by developing new sources of growth/profit in low/middle-income countries where harms are greater and policies weaker. Expansion into Africa, with South Africa (SA) as a gateway, is an explicit part of this strategy.
Many factors influence how much people drink, which vary from country-to-country: how easy/affordable is it to purchase alcohol, prevailing attitudes/ideas about drinking, where/what type of alcohol people usually drink? It is usually the country’s alcohol policy (i.e. regulations about when/where alcohol can be sold) and enforcement that determine these factors.
A research collaboration comprising the University of Cape Town, the South African Medical Research Council, Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and the University of Botswana will conduct the research in South Africa and Botswana from January 2025 to December 2029 focused on three sites in each of two provinces in South Africa (Khayelitsha, Klipfontein and Klapmuts in the Western Cape, and Atteridgeville, Olievenhoutbosch and Ga-Rankuwa in Gauteng) and three study sites in Botswana (Gaborone, Tlokweng and Francistown).
We will (1) review, consolidate, and synthesise existing literature on the influence of political, economic, and regulatory contexts on local alcohol environments, (2) iteratively map alcohol supply chains through documentary review and stakeholder engagement, (3) conduct a desk-based review of national and selected provincial and local laws, regulations and policies, and, in each study site, (4) map and describe alcohol outlets, (5) conduct interviews and (6) focus groups with vendors, alcohol consumers and non-drinking community members and in each South African study site (7) household surveys to understand the relationship between drinking patterns/behaviour and health/social outcomes. We will (8) apply modelled provincial alcohol harm estimates to derive harm reduction scenarios, (9) provide consolidated and accessible evidence for communities/policymakers to inform potential prevention interventions and (10) document the data requirements for effectively monitoring the alcohol environment.

This project has 6 objectives: 1) Examine business and political strategies the alcohol industry uses to influence policy and regulation at a global level before considering how these strategies are applied locally; 2) Describe the context in which people in South Africa and Botswana buy and consume alcohol and how this impacts on drinking patterns and behaviour. This will include mapping and visiting alcohol outlets, observing behaviour when buying/drinking, and interviewing people who sell and drink alcohol and those who do not. 3) Investigate how drinking patterns and behaviour impact health using existing data and data we collect in our study sites. By using mathematical models we will explore the possible impact of proposed interventions and policy changes on alcohol-related harm and consumption/sales in South Africa. 4) Harness community voices to influence alcohol policy by using research outputs that we co-create with community and policy stakeholders in South Africa and Botswana. 5) Strengthen capacity for both research through formal training (PhD and Masters students) and skills transfer, and 6) Through community engagement and involvement at the organisational and network levels.
